title: Find Longest Awesome Substring
description: Brute force to optimized: recounting digit frequencies versus a running parity bitmask with earliest occurrence lookups.

blocks.text: Given a string s made only of digits, find the length of the longest substring that is "awesome", meaning its digits can be rearranged to form a palindrome.

blocks.caption: A running parity bitmask, matched exactly or with one bit flipped, finds the longest awesome substring

blocks.text: Given a string s made only of digits, find the length of the longest substring that is "awesome", meaning its digits can be rearranged to form a palindrome.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Bag of Digit Tiles That Can Be Rearranged Symmetrically
blocks.text: Like checking whether a bag of numbered tiles pulled from a stretch of digits could be laid out symmetrically, which is possible exactly when at most one digit has an odd number of tiles, since that one odd digit can sit alone in the very middle.

blocks.caption: A substring is awesome exactly when its digits could be rearranged into a palindrome

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The substring \"24241\" has digit counts 2:2, 4:2, 1:1","only one digit (1) has an odd count, rearrangeable into a palindrome","A palindrome needs at most one character with an odd count, to sit alone in the middle; every other count must pair up symmetrically"],["Answer","5","\"24241\" is the longest substring in this string satisfying the at-most-one-odd-count condition"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The whole string has digit counts 1:2, 2:2, 3:2","every digit has an even count, rearrangeable into a palindrome","With every digit count even, the digits can pair up completely on both sides of the center with nothing left over"],["Answer","6","The entire string qualifies as awesome, so its full length is the answer"]]}

blocks.text: Every digit here appears exactly once, so any substring longer than a single character has at least two digits with an odd count (in fact, every digit in this string has an odd count of exactly 1), meaning no substring longer than 1 can be rearranged into a palindrome.

Before checking substrings directly, recognize that "can be rearranged into a palindrome" is a statement purely about counts, not positions, and a count's exact value never matters for this question, only whether it is odd or even.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A multiset of characters can be rearranged into a palindrome exactly when at most one character has an odd count, since every even-count character can split evenly on both sides of the center, leaving at most one leftover character to sit in the middle.

Observation 2: Whether a digit's count is odd or even is fully captured by a single bit, so the full "which digits have odd counts" state for any substring fits in a 10-bit number, one bit per digit 0 through 9.

Observation 3: Maintaining a running prefix bitmask via XOR (flip digit d's bit every time digit d is seen) means the parity of any substring is simply one prefix mask XOR another, since XOR-ing two prefixes cancels out everything before the substring starts.

Observation 4: The substring is awesome when that XOR is either exactly 0 (all even), or has exactly one bit set (exactly one odd digit), so for a fixed ending position, the question becomes "has this exact bitmask, or any bitmask one bit away from it, been seen before, and how early".

Whenever a condition on a substring depends only on the parity of counts over a small fixed alphabet, track a running XOR bitmask and look up matches, exact or within a small fixed number of bit flips, in a hash map of earliest occurrences.

This is the same prefix-XOR-plus-hashmap idea used for pure "all even" subarray or substring problems, extended here to also tolerate exactly one odd digit by checking all 10 possible single bit flips of the current mask.
Check every possible substring directly, count how many of its 10 possible digits have an odd frequency, and keep the longest one where at most one digit has an odd count.

items: For every starting and ending position, extract the substring.
Count the frequency of each of the 10 possible digits within it.
If at most one digit has an odd frequency, this substring is awesome, so track its length if it is the longest found so far.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: A fresh 10-element counts array is allocated for every single candidate substring, since each substring's digit frequencies are entirely independent of any other substring's.
odd_count is computed only after the full inner counting loop finishes, since a digit's true parity within this specific substring is only known once every one of its characters has been tallied.
best is only updated when odd_count is 0 or 1, directly encoding the palindrome-rearrangement condition as the acceptance test for each candidate.

blocks.text: Every substring's digit frequencies are directly counted, so every genuinely awesome substring is correctly identified.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared times 10), for every substring's frequency recount.
Space: O(10) for the counts of each candidate.

Limitation: recomputing digit frequencies from scratch for every candidate substring is wasteful, when a running prefix parity summary could answer the "at most one odd digit" question for any substring instantly.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force spends most of its time recomputing digit counts for overlapping substrings that share almost all of their characters, throwing that work away and starting fresh for the next candidate. But a substring's digit-count parity is really just the difference between two prefix states: everything counted from the start of the string up to its end, minus everything counted up to its start. Since only parity, odd or even, matters, that "difference" is exactly what XOR computes, flipping a bit for each occurrence and canceling pairs automatically. So instead of recomputing anything, maintain one running 10-bit bitmask as the string is scanned once, and for each position ask a lookup question rather than a recomputation question: has this exact bitmask been seen before, giving an all-even substring, or has a bitmask exactly one bit away been seen before, giving an exactly-one-odd substring? Both questions are answered by a hash map lookup per candidate bitmask, replacing an entire inner recount loop with O(1) amortized work.

Maintain a 10 bit running bitmask via prefix XOR, where bit d flips every time digit d is seen, so the bitmask at any position represents the parity (odd or even) of every digit's count from the start up to there. The substring between two positions has all even digit counts exactly when their two bitmasks are identical, and has exactly one odd digit count when their two bitmasks differ in exactly one bit. For every position, check the current bitmask against every previously seen bitmask that is either identical or differs by flipping exactly one of the 10 bits, using a hash map storing the earliest position each bitmask was ever seen at, to find the longest valid substring ending at that position.
Maintain a running 10 bit parity bitmask, and for each position check it and every single bit flip of it against the earliest occurrence of each bitmask seen so far.
Dry run for a small prefix of s = "3242415"

blocks.caption: Optimized: a running parity bitmask, matched exactly or with one bit flipped, against earliest occurrences

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n times 10), a single pass with 10 bit flip checks per position.
Space: O(2 to the power 10), since only 1024 possible bitmask values exist, bounding the hash map size.

One prefix mask XOR an earlier prefix mask cancels every digit's contribution from before that earlier position, leaving exactly the parity of each digit's count within the substring between them. That XOR result is 0 exactly when every digit's count in the substring is even, and has exactly one bit set exactly when exactly one digit has an odd count, both of which are precisely the palindrome-rearrangement condition, so checking those two cases against previously seen prefix masks correctly finds every awesome substring ending at the current position.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Current mask XOR earlier mask","Meaning for the substring between them"],"rows":[["Equal to 0","Every digit appears an even number of times: fully pairable into a palindrome with no middle character needed"],["Has exactly one bit set","Exactly one digit has an odd count: that digit can sit alone in the middle of a palindrome"],["Has two or more bits set","More than one digit has an odd count: not rearrangeable into a palindrome"]]}

items: first_seen is seeded with {0: -1} before the scan begins, so a substring that is awesome from the very first character (mask equals 0 already) can still correctly compute its length as i minus negative 1.
mask ^= (1 << digit) toggles exactly one bit per character processed, keeping the running bitmask an accurate parity summary of every digit seen so far.
The exact-match check and the 10 single-bit-flip checks are both evaluated at every position, together covering both the "all even" and "exactly one odd" acceptance conditions.
A bitmask is only ever recorded in first_seen the first time it appears, since an earlier occurrence always yields a longer or equal candidate substring than any later occurrence of that same mask.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (recount every substring)","O(n squared times 10)","O(10)","Every one of roughly n squared over 2 substrings pays its own O(10) frequency recount"],["Optimized (parity bitmask + earliest-occurrence map)","O(n times 10)","O(2 to the power 10)","A single pass, 10 flip-checks per position, bounded by the fixed 1024 possible bitmask values"]]}

blocks.text: The 10 bit parity bitmask compresses "which digits have odd counts so far" into a single small integer, and checking both an exact match and every single bit flip against previously seen values is the standard technique whenever a problem allows "all even" or "at most one odd" as valid conditions.

items: Forgetting to seed the earliest-seen map with bitmask 0 mapped to position -1, which silently drops every awesome substring that starts right at the beginning of the string.

Only checking for an exact bitmask match and forgetting the single bit flip check, which misses every valid substring that has exactly one odd digit count, a large and common category of awesome substrings.
Recording a bitmask's position every time it is seen instead of only the first time, which would use a later, shorter occurrence instead of the earliest, longest-substring-producing one.

items: Connect this problem explicitly to "Longest Substring with At Most K Distinct Characters" and other parity bitmask problems, since recognizing the bitmask-plus-hashmap-of-earliest-occurrence pattern is broadly reusable.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Can the characters be rearranged into a palindrome" points toward thinking about odd and even counts only, never positions; combined with a substring or subarray scan, that becomes a prefix-parity bitmask plus a hash map of earliest occurrences.

items: What if the alphabet were larger than 10 digits, say all 26 lowercase letters? The same technique works directly, just with a 26-bit mask and 26 single-bit-flip checks per position instead of 10.

What if the problem allowed up to k odd-count characters instead of just 1? Checking every combination of up to k bit flips grows combinatorially, so beyond a small fixed k this specific hash-map approach stops being efficient and a different technique is usually needed.

How would you also return one such longest awesome substring, not just its length? Store the actual substring boundaries alongside each bitmask's earliest position, and reconstruct the substring once the best pair of positions is found.
Same "condition depends only on parity of counts" insight as detecting palindrome-rearrangeable substrings and grouping-by-parity subarray problems.
Same prefix-XOR-plus-hashmap-of-earliest-occurrence technique as pure "subarray with all even counts" problems, just extended to tolerate one bit flip.
Same "check a small fixed number of bit flips per position" idea generalizes to any problem allowing a small fixed number of exceptions to an otherwise exact-match condition.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n squared times 10) time, O(10) space per candidate.
Optimized (parity bitmask with earliest occurrence map): O(n times 10) time, O(2 to the power 10) space.

items: Pattern: Prefix parity bitmask with earliest-occurrence hash map lookup, tolerating one bit flip
Core Idea: A substring can be rearranged into a palindrome exactly when at most one digit has an odd count, a condition captured entirely by comparing 10-bit prefix parity bitmasks
Time: O(10n)
Space: O(2 to the power 10), bounded by the fixed number of possible bitmask values

Most Important Observation: The palindrome-rearrangement condition depends only on count parity, letting an entire substring's digit-frequency state collapse into a single small bitmask compared via XOR
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Palindrome-able means at most one odd count; track parity as a bitmask, allow one bit flip
